---
title: "Migrating from gglaplot"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8.8, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 100,
  fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", out.width = "100%"
)
options(gglaplot2.font = "inter", rlib_message_verbosity = "quiet")
library(ggplot2)
library(gglaplot2)
```

gglaplot2 replaces gglaplot. Everything gglaplot exported is still here under
its old name, so a script written against it runs after changing one line:

```r
library(gglaplot2)
```

Each old name says once a session what it is now. The chart comes out in the
current style: the colours are the design tokens rather than the 2019 colour
tables, the type is the chart roles, and the marks are the ones the web charts
draw. The old arguments are translated, so `theme_gla(gla_theme = "inverse")`
is `theme_gla(theme = "dark")` and `gla_pal(palette_type = "highlight")` is
primary against context grey.

New code should use the new names. This page lists them side by side, then
rewrites gglaplot's own README example.

## How long the old names stay

For the whole 0.x series. A script that runs today runs on every 0.x
release. The last 0.x release turns the once-a-session note into a warning
on every call, and 1.0 removes the old names, so there is a release's notice
to move. The list below is what to move with.

## The names

| gglaplot | gglaplot2 | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `theme_gla(gla_theme = "inverse")` | `theme_gla(theme = "dark")` | |
| `theme_gla(x_axis_title = TRUE, y_axis_title = TRUE)` | `theme_gla(axis_titles = "both")` | The x title is on by default now, the y title off, as on the web charts |
| `theme_gla(xgridlines = TRUE)` | `theme_gla(gridlines = "both")` | `gridlines = "x"` for horizontal bars |
| `theme_gla(legend = FALSE)` | `theme_gla(legend = "none")` | |
| `theme_gla(y_label_length = , free_y_facets = )` | nothing | Tick labels sit beside the axis |
| `gla_pal(palette_type = "categorical", n = 3)` | `gla_pal("categorical", 3)` or `scale_colour_gla()` | |
| `gla_pal(palette_type = "highlight", n = c(1, 1))` | `scale_colour_gla()` | London against a comparator is primary against context by the level names |
| `gla_pal(palette_type = "quantitative")` | `gla_pal("sequential")` or `scale_fill_gla_c()` | |
| `gla_pal(palette_type = "diverging")` | `gla_pal("diverging")` or `scale_fill_gla_b("diverging")` | Stepped and counted out from zero; `scale_fill_gla_c("diverging")` for a smooth ramp |
| `gla_pal(main_colours = "ldndkpink")` | `gla_token("data-categorical-darkpink")` | The colour names are translated |
| `ggla_line()` | `geom_gla_line()` | |
| `ggla_highlight(filter_type = "end")` | `geom_gla_endpoint()` | `where` takes `"end"`, `"start"`, `"max"`, `"min"` |
| `ggla_highlight(geom = GeomGLATextHighlight)` | `geom_gla_endlabel()` | Labels push apart when they overlap |
| `ggla_labelline(y1 = )` | `gla_reference_line(y = , label = )` | `x = ` for a vertical rule |
| `ggla_axisat0()` | `gla_zero_line()` | With `expand_limits(y = 0)` if the axis does not reach zero |
| `ggla_highlightarea()` | `annotate_gla_range()` | |
| `ggla_horizbar()` | `geom_gla_col()` with the category on `y`, `theme_gla(gridlines = "x")` | No `coord_flip()` |
| `ggla_sf()` | `geom_gla_sf()` | |
| `ggla_donut()` | `ggla_donut()` | Kept as it was, on the tokens |
| `annotate(geom = GeomGLAAnnotate)` | `geom_gla_text()` or `annotate(geom = GeomGlaText)` | |
| `show_gla_pals()` | `gla_show_pal()` | |
| `left_align_labs()` | nothing | `theme_gla()` aligns the titles to the plot edge |
| `mm_to_pt` | `mm_to_pt` | One CSS pixel in millimetres; the theme sets the widths now |
| `gla_default$background` | `gla_token("chart-surface")` | The old lists are generated from the tokens |
| `gla_colours$blue_core` | `gla_token("data-categorical-blue")` | |
| `ggla_plotly_settings()` | `ggla_plotly_settings()` | Kept, on the tokens; `ggplotly()` understands the `geom_gla_*()` marks |
| `labs(caption = "Source: ...")` | `gla_labs(source = , note = , byline = )` | |

## gglaplot's example, both ways

gglaplot's README drew the gender pay gap for London and the UK. As written,
it runs:

```{r old, fig.height = 4.4}
pal <- gla_pal(gla_theme = "default", palette_type = "highlight", n = c(1, 1))

ggplot(LDNUK, aes(x = Year, y = GPG, group = location, colour = location)) +
  ggla_line(aes(linewidth = location)) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(4 * mm_to_pt, 2 * mm_to_pt)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  ggla_highlight(filter_type = "end") +
  ggla_axisat0() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, 32.5),
                     labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "'%y",
               expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.01))) +
  labs(title = "Gender Pay Gap - Total (Median)",
       subtitle = "Gender Pay Gap - Total (Median) - London VS UK",
       caption = "Note: 2017 data is provisional\nChart: GLA City Intelligence  Source: London Datastore") +
  theme_gla(gla_theme = "default")
```

The same chart in gglaplot2. The scale reads the level names, so London is
primary and the UK context grey without a palette being built; the lines end
in a marker and a label instead of a legend; the title states the finding and
the footer carries the byline, source and note.

```{r new, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot(LDNUK, aes(x = Year, y = GPG, colour = location)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  geom_gla_endpoint() +
  geom_gla_endlabel(aes(label = location)) +
  gla_zero_line() +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), limits = c(0, 32.5), expand = c(0, 0),
                     labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "'%y",
               expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))) +
  gla_labs(
    title = "London's gender pay gap has narrowed less than the UK's",
    subtitle = "Median gender pay gap, all employees",
    source = "London Datastore", note = "2017 data is provisional",
    byline = "GLA City Intelligence", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla(legend = "none")
```

## What changed underneath

- Colour comes from the design tokens the visualisation team publish, read
  by name with `gla_token()`. `gla_default`, `gla_inverse` and `gla_colours`
  are generated from them, so `gla_colours$blue_core` is the token that
  colour is now, not the 2019 hex.
- The categorical palette is the web charts' order and has eight colours.
  Three is the design ceiling; past it, label the series directly.
- `theme_gla()` needs ggplot2 4.0 or later: the marks read their colour,
  width and type from the theme, which is what lets `theme_gla(theme =
  "dark")` recolour a chart without a change to the layers.
- Inter, the design system's typeface, is bundled and used wherever the
  device can draw it. See the Typography page.
- The old package's chroma fork and its dependencies on dplyr, tidyr,
  checkmate and ggplotify are gone. plotly is suggested, not required.
